name: Skunk oil

card.summary: A traditional North American folk balm of rendered skunk fat, used as an emollient on dry or chapped skin and rubbed on the chest.
card.note: No peer-reviewed studies of its safety or effect on skin; risks are inferred from similar animal fats.

quick.overview:
Skunk oil is fat rendered from the back of the striped skunk. Indigenous peoples and later settlers in North America used it as a balm or liniment for chapped or irritated skin and for chest complaints, and it has a smooth, emollient texture.

Its appearance link is through skin comfort: traditional accounts describe it softening dry, chapped or chafed skin. Wikipedia and Grokipedia report that the uses rest on historical and anecdotal accounts, with no peer-reviewed studies of it.
quick.how: Traditionally the fat was boiled down into a butter-like oil and rubbed onto the skin or chest. Today it is mainly sold by wildlife supply companies for trapping, with some small-batch salves marketed for muscle relief.
quick.risks: Grokipedia states that irritation or rashes are possible, rare severe reactions in people with alpha-gal syndrome, and trace thiols from improper rendering; it says these risks are inferred from similar animal fats, not from studies of skunk oil.

lead: Skunk oil, also called skunk grease, is fat rendered from the two lateral fat deposits along a skunk's back. It has little of the odour of skunk spray.[1] It was used as a healing balm or liniment by Native Americans and later by frontier settlers.[1][2]

Accounts describe it as moisturising and soothing for dry, chapped or chafed skin and irritations such as poison ivy rashes, among Mi'kmaq, Delaware and Lakota groups, in addition to its better-known use rubbed on the chest for colds.[2] Its warm, emollient feel is attributed to its fat content.[1][2]
Wikipedia says the traditional claims rest on history and anecdote and that its Uses section lacks citations; Grokipedia says there are no peer-reviewed studies on its safety or efficacy.[1][2]

chain: Rendered skunk fat applied to skin
Softer, less chapped skin, as described in traditional accounts
angle.text: Folk accounts use it as an emollient for chapped and dry skin. As with other animal fats, the moisturising effect is attributed to its oil content rather than to tested results.

infobox: Rendered fat of the striped skunk (Mephitis mephitis)
Pale yellow oil, semi-solid when cool
Trapping and wildlife supply; niche salves

paras: The oil is made by slowly rendering subcutaneous fat from along the back of the striped skunk, where animals build up reserves in late summer and fall.[2] Wikipedia compares its consistency to motor oil and notes a mild warming sensation on the skin.[1] Grokipedia reports that it is mostly triglycerides, with a higher iodine value than lard and natural antioxidants such as tocopherols.[2]

Wikipedia says early explorers and fur traders valued skunk oil in medical kits, that around 1900 Maine reportedly produced about 25,000 gallons a year, and that farmers made it at home by boiling the fat.[1] Mid-nineteenth-century recipe books such as Dr. Chase's Recipes included it in liniments, and use declined in the 1920s as mass-produced products replaced it, according to Grokipedia.[2]

Reported skin uses include soothing rashes, preventing chapping and treating dry skin and chafing in cold climates.[2] Today it is sold in glass jars by wildlife supply companies for use as a trapping lure base and waterproofing agent, and in a few salves blended with eucalyptus and menthol.[2] Some hunters use it to mask human scent.[1]

Grokipedia lists possible skin irritation from residual proteins, rare severe reactions in people with alpha-gal syndrome, possible irritation from trace thiols if rendering is poor, and digestive upset if swallowed. It states these are inferred from similar animal fats, not from studies of skunk oil.[2]
